lessons.title: segunda to sexta — the week that got numbered
lessons.gloss: the weekdays (Mon–Fri) — Portuguese NUMBERS its days instead of naming planets

segments.text: Here Portuguese does something no other Romance language does. French, Italian, and Spanish all name their weekdays for planet-gods (lundi, lunedì, lunes = the Moon). Portuguese threw the pagan gods out and numbered the days instead — and the numbers are the very ones you just learned.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: The story: a bishop renames the week

segments.text: In the 6th century, Martinho de Braga, a bishop in what is now northern Portugal, refused to let Christians name days after Mars and Jupiter. Borrowing the Church's word for the numbered holy days of Easter week, he called them feiras — and Portuguese alone kept the system for every week.
feira from Latin fēria, "a feast-day / a day free of work." (The same fēria drifted, elsewhere, into "market/fair" — English fair is its cousin, because markets were held on feast-days.)

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 5 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: Portuguese, means, from ordinal of, (cardinal you learned). Come back and look at it when you have stopped.

So quarta-feira is literally "fourth feast-day," and you can hear quatro (4) inside quarta. In everyday speech the "-feira" is often dropped: "Até segunda!" — "See you Monday!" (Why does Monday start at two, not one? Because Sunday is counted as the first day — the next lesson closes that loop.)

segments.instruction: "segunda, terça, quarta, quinta, sexta" — Monday through Friday
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "segunda, terça, quarta, quinta, sexta" — Monday through Friday]

segments.instruction: hear the number in each — "quarta from quatro (4), quinta from cinco (5), sexta from seis (6)"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: hear the number in each — "quarta ← quatro (4), quinta ← cinco (5), sexta ← seis (6)"]

segments.instruction: drop the tail — "Até sexta!" ("See you Friday!")
segments.source: [YOU SAY: drop the tail — "Até sexta!" ("See you Friday!")]

segments.text: How is Portuguese unique among Romance languages here? (It numbers its weekdays — feiras — instead of naming planet-gods.) What does feira mean, and its English cousin? ("Feast-day," from fēria; English fair.) What number hides in quinta-feira? (Five — quinta from quintus, cousin of cinco.) Next: the two days that kept their old names — sábado and domingo.

lessons.title: sábado and domingo — and why Monday is "the second"
lessons.gloss: the weekend (Saturday, Sunday) — the two days that kept their names

needs: your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The two days, taken apart until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Five weekdays got numbered — but two kept their names. Sábado and domingo are the religious anchors of the Portuguese week, and domingo is the key that explains why the counting started where it did.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 2 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: Portuguese, from Latin, meaning, shared with. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
sábado is the Sabbath, from Hebrew shabbāt "to rest" — the one weekend name every Romance language shares (even numbering-mad Portuguese kept it).
domingo is "the Lord's day," diēs Dominica, from Dominus "lord, master" ( becomes English dominion, dominate, dame).

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: domingo is "day one" — so Monday is "day two"

segments.text: Now the loop closes. The Church counted domingo (Sunday) as the first day of the week — prima feria, the Lord's day, the start. That's why:
domingo = 1st becomes segunda-feira (Monday) = 2nd becomes terça (3rd) becomes … becomes sexta (Friday) = 6th becomes sábado (Saturday) = 7th.

Monday isn't the first weekday in this system — it's the day after the Lord's day, the second. So segunda-feira ("second feast-day") makes perfect sense once you know Sunday was counted first. The whole week is a countdown anchored on domingo.

segments.instruction: the full week — "domingo, segunda, terça, quarta, quinta, sexta, sábado"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the full week — "domingo, segunda, terça, quarta, quinta, sexta, sábado"]

segments.instruction: the anchors — "sábado = Sabbath, domingo = the Lord's day"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the anchors — "sábado = Sabbath, domingo = the Lord's day"]

segments.instruction: the logic — "domingo is 1st, so segunda (Monday) is 2nd"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the logic — "domingo is 1st, so segunda (Monday) is 2nd"]

segments.text: Give all seven Portuguese days. (Domingo, segunda … sábado.) What does domingo mean, and why does that make Monday "segunda"? ("The Lord's day"; Sunday is counted first, so Monday is the second.) Which weekend name do all the Romance languages share? (Sábado — the Sabbath.) Next chapter builds on this toward telling the time.
